Name / Question / Prompt: The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet it is solid. Why?
Description / Options: A) It is made of rock, not metal | B) Enormous pressure keeps the iron from melting | C) It is cooling faster than the outer core
Correct Answer: B) Enormous pressure keeps the iron from melting
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): What else increases as you go deeper, besides temperature?
Explanation (Why): Pressure raises the melting point of iron. At the centre the pressure is over three million times that at the surface, so iron stays solid even near 5,000 °C.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the soft, slowly flowing layer that tectonic plates glide over.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It sits just below the rigid shell.
Explanation (Why): The asthenosphere is close to its melting point, so it is weak and can flow. That lets the rigid plates above it move a few centimetres a year.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the rigid shell that is broken into tectonic plates.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It includes the crust and the very top of the mantle.
Explanation (Why): Plates are pieces of lithosphere, not just crust. Nigeria rides on the African Plate.

Correct Answer: B) No, it is solid rock that is weak enough to flow very slowly
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Earthquake S-waves do travel through it, only more slowly.
Explanation (Why): The asthenosphere is mostly solid. Only a tiny fraction may be melted. It behaves like very stiff putty over long time spans.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the mid-ocean ridge, where new ocean floor forms.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Look for the highest ground in the middle.
Explanation (Why): Hot, young lithosphere at the ridge is buoyant, so it stands high. As it moves away it cools, shrinks and sinks lower.

Name / Question / Prompt: The magnetic stripes are mirror images on both sides of the ridge. What does that tell you?
Description / Options: A) The ridge is where the crust is oldest | B) New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides, recording each magnetic reversal | C) Ocean currents painted the stripes
Correct Answer: B) New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides, recording each magnetic reversal
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Think about where the newest basalt cools and locks in the magnetic field, then which way the plates move.
Explanation (Why): Symmetrical stripes were the key evidence for sea-floor spreading in the 1960s. They let geologists date the ocean floor without drilling.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the molten rock that fills the gap as the plates pull apart.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It glows.
Explanation (Why): As hot mantle rises, the pressure on it drops and it partly melts. This decompression melting makes the basalt of every ocean floor.

Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It is where the ocean plate starts to bend down.
Explanation (Why): Trenches mark where a plate bends and dives into the mantle. The Mariana Trench is about 11 km deep.

Name / Question / Prompt: Why does the oceanic plate sink instead of the continental one?
Description / Options: A) Oceanic lithosphere is denser | B) It is moving faster | C) Continents are attached to the core
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Compare basalt with granite.
Explanation (Why): Old oceanic lithosphere is colder and denser than the asthenosphere below, so it sinks under its own weight. Continental crust is too buoyant.

Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Look on the continent, above the sinking slab.
Explanation (Why): The slab releases water as it heats up. Water lowers the melting point of the mantle wedge above, producing magma that rises to feed a line of volcanoes.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the earthquakes that trace the sinking plate.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Small yellow dots along the slab.
Explanation (Why): Earthquakes happen only in rock that is cold and brittle enough to break. Their deepening line maps the slab hundreds of kilometres into the mantle.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the part of the fault where the plates slide past each other in opposite directions.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It is the segment between the two ridge pieces. Watch the arrows.
Explanation (Why): Only the segment between the offset ridges is an active transform boundary. Earthquakes cluster here.

Name / Question / Prompt: Along a transform boundary, crust is…
Description / Options: A) created | B) destroyed | C) neither created nor destroyed
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): The plates only slide sideways past each other.
Explanation (Why): Transform boundaries just move crust sideways. California's San Andreas Fault is a famous continental example.

Variant / View: waves (Waves from a fault); shadow (Shadow zones)
Description / Options: Watch P- and S-waves race out from a fault, then see the shadow zones that revealed the liquid core.
Explanation (Why): Nigeria sits far from plate boundaries, but small tremors do happen, for example around Kwoi in Kaduna State in 2016 and in Mpape, Abuja, in 2018.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the focus, where the rupture began.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It glows, deep on the fault plane.
Explanation (Why): Most earthquakes start within the top 20 km of the crust. Some in subduction zones start 700 km down.

Name / Question / Prompt: Watch the two wave fronts. Which will reach the seismograph station first?
Description / Options: A) The S-wave | B) The P-wave | C) Both at the same time
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Compare how fast each ring grows.
Explanation (Why): P-waves travel about 1.7 times faster than S-waves. The further the station, the bigger the gap between their arrivals, which is how seismologists measure distance.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the region where no direct S-waves arrive.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Correct Answer: S-wave shadow zone [sshadow] OR P-wave shadow zone [pshadow]
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It is on the far side of the planet from the earthquake.
Explanation (Why): The S-wave shadow zone covers everything beyond about 103°. Its size let Richard Oldham and others work out the size of the core.

Name / Question / Prompt: Why is there a huge S-wave shadow zone?
Description / Options: A) S-waves are too weak to travel far | B) S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core | C) The inner core reflects them
Correct Answer: B) S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): S-waves shear rock side to side. What can a liquid not resist?
Explanation (Why): Liquids have no shear strength, so shear waves cannot pass through them. That is our main evidence that the outer core is liquid.

Description / Options: Close an ocean, crash two continents together and watch a mountain belt rise with a deep root beneath it.
Explanation (Why): About 600 million years ago, the Pan-African orogeny joined West Africa to other continental blocks to build Gondwana. Nigeria's Basement Complex gneisses, schists and Older Granites are the deeply eroded roots of that mountain belt. The Himalaya is the same process happening today.

Description / Options: Thick, buoyant continental crust riding on its plate.

The narrowing ocean between the two continents.

Denser rock that the continental crust floats on.

Name / Question / Prompt: Start the slider at 0 and move it right. What has to disappear before two continents can collide?
Description / Options: A) A mountain range | B) The ocean between them, by subduction | C) The mantle
Correct Answer: B) The ocean between them, by subduction
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Watch the blue area in the middle.
Explanation (Why): Oceanic crust is dense enough to sink, so the ocean closes by subduction. Continental crust is too buoyant to sink far, so when the continents meet they crumple instead.

Name / Question / Prompt: With the slider past 70%, tap the crustal root under the mountains.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Look at the bottom of the crust, below the peaks.
Explanation (Why): Isostasy: thick crust floats higher and sinks deeper, like a thick block of wood in water. The Himalayan crust is about 70 km thick, twice the normal thickness.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the suture where the two continents joined.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): The dark line in the middle of the mountain belt.
Explanation (Why): Sutures mark former oceans. Geologists find them by looking for slivers of ocean-floor rock (ophiolites) squeezed between two continents.

Name / Question / Prompt: The Basement Complex of Nigeria is mostly gneiss and schist, flat-lying at the surface today. What does that tell you?
Description / Options: A) It was always flat | B) It is the deeply eroded root of an ancient mountain belt | C) It formed in a desert
Correct Answer: B) It is the deeply eroded root of an ancient mountain belt
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Where in a colliding mountain belt are rocks squeezed and heated enough to turn into gneiss?
Explanation (Why): Metamorphic rocks like gneiss form deep in mountain roots. Hundreds of millions of years of erosion removed the peaks and exposed the root.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap a chloride ion. It is the larger of the two.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Compare the sizes of the two colours.
Explanation (Why): Chloride ions are much bigger than sodium ions. The small Na⁺ ions fit into the gaps between them.

Name / Question / Prompt: Drag the slider to split the crystal. Halite always breaks along flat planes at right angles. Why?
Description / Options: A) Its ions form a cubic grid, so the weakest planes meet at 90° | B) Salt is very soft | C) It was cut by a machine
Correct Answer: A) Its ions form a cubic grid, so the weakest planes meet at 90°
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Look at how the ions are lined up in rows.
Explanation (Why): This is cleavage: breaking along planes of weak bonding set by the crystal structure. Halite has three cleavage planes at right angles, so it breaks into cubes.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the silicon atom at the centre of the tetrahedron.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It is the small atom in the middle.
Explanation (Why): The SiO₄ tetrahedron is the building block of all silicate minerals, the most common minerals in the crust.

Name / Question / Prompt: Quartz has no cleavage. It breaks along curved, glassy surfaces. Why?
Description / Options: A) Its bonds are equally strong in every direction, so there is no weak plane | B) It is too soft to cleave | C) It is made of sheets like mica
Correct Answer: A) Its bonds are equally strong in every direction, so there is no weak plane
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Every oxygen links two tetrahedra, in all three dimensions.
Explanation (Why): With no weak direction, quartz breaks with a curved conchoidal fracture, like thick glass.

Name / Question / Prompt: Drag the slider to peel the sheets. Why does mica split into thin, flexible sheets?
Description / Options: A) The silicate sheets are held to each other by weak bonds | B) It is full of gas bubbles | C) Mica is a metal
Correct Answer: A) The silicate sheets are held to each other by weak bonds
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Compare the bonding inside a sheet with the bonding between sheets.
Explanation (Why): Mica has perfect basal cleavage: strong bonds within each sheet, weak bonds between them. You can peel it with a fingernail.

Description / Options: Tap on 3D model

Explanation (Why): Each sheet is a two-dimensional network of linked tetrahedra.

Explanation (Why): The schist belts of the Nigerian Basement Complex, such as the Ilesha schist belt with its gold deposits, and the surrounding gneisses record Pan-African metamorphism.

Name / Question / Prompt: Start at the left of the slider and move right slowly. Which rock forms first from shale?
Description / Options: A) Gneiss | B) Slate | C) Schist
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Watch the rock name under the slider.
Explanation (Why): Low-grade metamorphism of shale gives slate, then phyllite, schist and finally gneiss as heat and pressure rise.

Name / Question / Prompt: Under directed pressure (squeezing), how do mica flakes line up at high metamorphic grade?
Description / Options: A) Parallel to the squeeze | B) Perpendicular to the squeeze | C) Randomly
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Imagine pressing flat coins or flakes between your palms. Which way do their flat faces turn?
Explanation (Why): Platy minerals grow and rotate until they lie at right angles to the greatest pressure. That alignment is foliation.

Explanation (Why): Index minerals like garnet let geologists map zones of metamorphic grade across a region.

Explanation (Why): Magma rises because it is less dense than the rock around it, and pools where it stops being buoyant.

Name / Question / Prompt: Shield volcanoes are very wide with gentle slopes. Why?
Description / Options: A) Their basalt lava is runny and flows a long way before it cools | B) They are built from loose ash | C) They erupt only once
Correct Answer: A) Their basalt lava is runny and flows a long way before it cools
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Think about how thick or runny the lava is.
Explanation (Why): Low-silica basalt has low viscosity, so it spreads in thin flows over huge distances. Hawaii's Mauna Loa is the classic example.

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the conduit that magma rises through.
Description / Options: Tap on 3D model
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): A narrow pipe connecting the chamber to the summit.
Explanation (Why): In stratovolcanoes sticky magma can plug the conduit, letting pressure build until it erupts explosively.

Name / Question / Prompt: This volcano is steep and built of alternating lava and ash layers. What does that tell you about its magma?
Description / Options: A) It is runny basalt that erupts gently | B) It is sticky, gas-rich magma that switches between explosive and lava eruptions | C) It has no magma
Correct Answer: B) It is sticky, gas-rich magma that switches between explosive and lava eruptions
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Ash comes from explosions. What makes magma explode?
Explanation (Why): Andesitic magma is viscous and traps gas, so stratovolcanoes alternate between ash-rich explosions and thick lava flows that pile up steeply.

Name / Question / Prompt: Cinder cones are small and steep, and can grow in just a few years. What are they built from?
Description / Options: A) Thick lava flows | B) Loose fragments of frothy lava (scoria) thrown from a vent | C) Ice and mud
Correct Answer: B) Loose fragments of frothy lava (scoria) thrown from a vent
Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Think about what gas-rich blobs of lava become when blasted into the air and piled around a vent.
Explanation (Why): Gas-rich blobs of lava are blasted out, cool in the air and land around the vent, piling up at the steepest angle loose gravel can hold, about 30–35°.

Name / Question / Prompt: Unlike Hawaii, volcanoes along the Cameroon Line show no steady age pattern. What does that suggest?

Name / Question / Prompt: Tap the sheet that runs parallel to the layers.

Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): It is flat and lies between two beds.

Hint (Wrong 1st Attempt): Can you cut through something that does not exist yet?
Explanation (Why): The principle of cross-cutting relationships: anything that cuts through a rock is younger than the rock it cuts.
